Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside them, a lender can still require it.

50.2% of North Dakota's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 50.2% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

How much does it cost here?

Typically about $856 a year ($71 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $614 and $1,266. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $614 · Typical $856 · A quarter pay over $1,266 · A tenth pay $1,589 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 4,281 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price; a brand-new policy is priced at full risk.

Coverage in force: $1.3 billion of building and $411.5 million of contents coverage across all North Dakota policies.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy, but there is no wait if you buy it with a new or refinanced mortgage.

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, or change coverage at renewal; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. If FEMA aid pays to repair a home in a high-risk zone, you must buy and keep flood insurance on it, or you cannot get that aid again after a later flood. Past aid paid here is in “Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?” below.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, fema.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Floods here have led to 13,307 NFIP flood claims and $259.0 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 1997, 2011 and 2009.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 1997 ($97,373,408), 2011 ($96,448,339), 2009 ($20,976,952). Total paid $259,025,707: net building + contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

That is 13,307 claims since 1978 against 5,784 policy units in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~48 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2025; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Do flood claims here actually pay out?

Most do: 81.5% of claims here paid something. The average paid claim was $23,924.

  • Average paid claim, incl. code-upgrade (ICC) pay$23,924
  • Closed with no payment18.5%
  • Claims that paid10,839

FEMA lists reasons a claim closes without payment, such as damage below the deductible, no flood as the policy defines it, or seepage and drain backup the policy does not cover. The average is over claims that paid something and includes Increased Cost of Compliance payments (help to elevate or rebuild to code), which the yearly totals above leave out. Dollars are as paid at the time, not adjusted for inflation; a single home can file across several floods over the years.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2025; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for 31.9% of the 2,929 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 2,929 policies reporting one)31.9%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)72.1%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 9,409 claims paid with a damage figure)11.7%

Rebuilding cost is the replacement-cost figure on single-family primary-home policies that report one; many owners insure to the building maximum even when that figure is lower, so the two shares measure different things. The damage share counts every paid claim with a damage figure, all building types.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Why do sites quote different prices for North Dakota?

Because they measure different things. Existing single-family policies here typically cost $856 a year, but a new one is priced at full risk: about $906 with fees.

MeasureAmountWhat it counts
Typical cost, single-family homes (median)$856premium plus fees; the middle policy
Typical premium only$664before the federal fee, reserve fund and surcharge
Typical cost, policies whose term began in 2025$8681,466 policies
Typical cost, policies whose term began in 2026$8452,815 policies
FEMA's full-risk premium (median)$692the price FEMA's model sets; new policies start here
Full-risk premium plus average fees$906close to what a new single-family policy pays
Average (mean) cost, single-family homes$1,003pulled up by a few expensive policies
Average cost, every policy type$1,123adds condos, rentals and businesses

All from the NFIP policies in force on July 31, 2026. Published figures rarely say which of these they are, or which year; private flood insurance is not in this data. Policies renew on their own anniversaries, so the latest year shows where renewals are heading.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

43.3% of policies here pay less than FEMA's full-risk price, so their bills are rising toward it. Median premium $664, full-risk $692 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$664
  • Median full-risk premium$692
  • Pay below full-risk43.3% of 4,281

Yearly cap: Those prices step up toward full-risk each year, limited by the yearly cap. By law a primary home's premium cannot rise more than 18% a year; some policies, such as second homes and businesses, can rise up to 25%. The cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. Bills already at full risk still change with FEMA's yearly rate updates.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Do the same homes flood again here?

Yes: FEMA's disaster-aid records hold 1,940 damage records from homes here that flooded more than once; 8 records are from homes on FEMA's severe repetitive loss list.

  • Repeat-flood damage records1,940
  • Records from homes on the severe repetitive loss list8

One home appears once for each declared disaster that damaged it, so this counts damage events on repeat-flooded homes, not distinct homes (FEMA says these records cannot be totaled by property). Disaster-aid records since 2002, separate from NFIP insurance claims.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Individual Assistance Multiple-Loss Flood Properties. Data: FEMA's current multiple-loss list; retrieved October 26, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $98.9 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $7,036 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Hurricane aid includes wind damage. COVID, fire, ice-storm and tornado aid are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Are these counts complete?

Every record FEMA's download lists was received and counted. FEMA also publishes a separate official policy count, which we have not yet compared for North Dakota.

In-force count: 5,784 policy units (from 5,730 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). Download check: policies: 5,730 of 5,730 fetched; claims: 13,307 of 13,307 fetched.

What these records cannot tell you (your own premium, private prices, your exact zone) is on the methodology page.
